title: Deadlines you set yourself help, but evenly spaced ones help more
body: MIT students had to hand in three papers. Those given evenly spaced deadlines scored best. Those allowed to choose their own did better than those with a single final deadline, but most spaced them too late to get the full benefit.
takeaway: Break big work into dated chunks, and ask someone else to hold you to the dates.
visual: a long road at dusk with three evenly spaced glowing milestones leading toward a distant finish gate

title: Walking raises creative output by about 60%
body: In Stanford experiments, people thought of more original uses for everyday objects while walking than while sitting, about 60% more on average. It worked on a treadmill facing a blank wall too, and the boost lingered for a while after they sat down.
takeaway: Take a problem that needs ideas for a walk. For problems with one right answer, sitting was just as good.
source: Oppezzo & Schwartz, Journal of Experimental Psychology: LMC (2014)
visual: a person walking along a tree-lined path with a trail of small glowing shapes rising from their footsteps

title: The 10,000-hour rule is not a rule
body: The figure comes from a 1993 study of violinists, where 10,000 hours was an average and not a threshold. A 2014 review of 88 studies found that deliberate practice explained about 26% of skill differences in games, 21% in music and 18% in sports.
takeaway: Practice matters a great deal, but no fixed number of hours guarantees mastery.
visual: a violinist practising alone in a dim room with a large hourglass beside them, its sand only partly run through

title: Mixing up practice feels worse and works better
body: Students learned to calculate the volumes of four shapes. One group practised one shape at a time. The other had the problems shuffled. On a test a week later the shuffled group scored 63% and the one-at-a-time group scored 20%.
takeaway: Shuffle problem types when you practise. Choosing the right method is part of the skill.
visual: four different geometric solids tumbling together in mid-air above a desk, lit from one side

title: The idea that willpower drains like a battery did not hold up
body: A famous 1998 experiment suggested that resisting temptation uses up a limited store of willpower. In 2016, 23 laboratories repeated a standard version of the test with more than 2,000 people and found an effect close to zero.
takeaway: Be wary of tidy stories about willpower as a fuel tank. Removing temptation from your surroundings is a safer bet.
source: Hagger et al., Perspectives on Psychological Science (2016)
visual: a glowing battery-shaped lantern on a table that turns out to be an ordinary glass jar with a candle inside

title: The marshmallow test predicts less than you were told
body: In the original studies, children who waited for a second marshmallow did better as teenagers. A 2018 repeat with over 900 children from more varied homes found the link was about half as strong, and most of it vanished once family background was taken into account.
takeaway: A child's patience reflects their circumstances as much as their character. Be slow to read destiny into one test.
visual: a single marshmallow on a plate in front of a small child's folded hands at a plain table, warm light from a window

title: New weeks, months and birthdays make people start things
body: Researchers tracked gym visits, internet searches for the word diet and pledges on a goal-setting website. All of them jumped at the start of a week, a month, a year or a term, and just after birthdays. They named it the fresh start effect.
takeaway: Use the next landmark date to begin, and build the habit before the clean-slate feeling fades.
visual: a blank page of a diary lit by sunrise through a window, a pair of running shoes waiting on the floor beside it

title: You remember an experience by its peak and its end
body: Patients having a colonoscopy rated their pain every minute. Their later memory of it tracked the worst moment and the final minutes, not the total. A longer procedure that ended gently was remembered as less unpleasant than a shorter one that ended badly.
takeaway: End things well: a meeting, a workout, a holiday. The ending shapes the memory, and the memory decides if you return.
visual: a mountain trail seen from the side with one high sharp peak and a gentle golden slope down to a calm lake at the end

title: Once you know something, you cannot imagine not knowing it
body: In a 1990 experiment, people tapped out well-known songs on a table while listeners tried to name them. The tappers predicted that listeners would get half right. Listeners named 3 songs out of 120. The tappers could hear the tune in their heads.
takeaway: When you explain something, assume your listener hears only the tapping. Give the context you think is obvious.
source: Elizabeth Newton, Stanford University doctoral dissertation (1990)
visual: a hand tapping a rhythm on a wooden table, music visibly swirling in the tapper's head while the listener opposite sees only ripples

title: People notice you far less than you think
body: Students were asked to walk into a room of classmates wearing an embarrassing T-shirt. They guessed that about half the room had noticed it. In fact about a quarter had. Psychologists call the gap the spotlight effect.
takeaway: Most people are busy thinking about themselves. Your mistakes are less visible than they feel.
source: Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (2000)
visual: a figure standing under an imagined spotlight in a busy room where everyone else is absorbed in their own small pools of light
